unit.can_do_en: book a visit and describe where it hurts.

brief.situation_en: Maria calls the health centre. Satu is a nurse.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Moi! Mä tarviin lääkärin. Mun kurkkuun sattuu.
lines.text_kirja: Hei! Minä tarvitsen lääkärin. Minun kurkkuuni sattuu.
lines.gloss_en: Hi! I need a doctor. My throat hurts.

judge.reason: Only register differences (moi/hei, mä/minä, tarviin/tarvitsen, mun/minun); same meaning.
Kauanks/kauanko and sattunu/sattunut are register variants; same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Kolme päivää. Ja mul on kuumetta.
lines.text_kirja: Kolme päivää. Ja minulla on kuumetta.
lines.gloss_en: Three days. And I have a fever.

judge.reason: Mul/minulla is a register difference; three days and fever are the same.
Onks sun/onko sinun are register variants; same question about difficulty swallowing.
Joo and kyllä both mean yes; 'a little' is kept.

lines.speaker: Satu
lines.text_puhe: Okei. Lääkäri voi nähä sut huomenna kymmeneltä.
lines.text_kirja: Selvä. Lääkäri voi nähdä sinut huomenna kymmeneltä.
lines.gloss_en: OK. The doctor can see you tomorrow at ten.

judge.reason: Okei/selvä, nähä/nähdä, sut/sinut are register differences; tomorrow at ten is unchanged.
Kiitti/kiitos are register variants of thanks.

forms.why_en: This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'here', telling where she is new.
Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Adds -n for 'I': tarvita becomes tarvitsen. Speech says tarviin.
As the thing you need, lääkäri takes -n: lääkärin.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: illative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Adds -un for 'into' and -ni for 'my': kurkku becomes kurkkuuni. Speech drops -ni: kurkkuun.
Sattua 'to hurt' doubles its last vowel for 'it': sattuu. People say it the same way.
Kauan, long, with -ko to ask. Speech says -ks: kauanks.
The illative singular of se 'it': siihen, 'into it, for it'. People say it the same way.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
From sattua, to hurt. After 'on' this form says something has gone on until now. Speech drops the t: sattunu.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
'Day.' The set phrase hyvää päivää 'good day' uses the partitive singular; here it says goodbye politely.
And: joins the coffee and the bun in the order.
Minä with -lla. With on it means 'I have'. Speech shortens it to mul.
The partitive singular is used for an illness you have: kuume becomes kuumetta.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Means 'is...?'. The question ending -ko turns 'on' (is) into a question.
Sinä with -n for 'your': sinun. Speech shortens it to sun.
Speech turns the ea at the end into ee: vaikea becomes vaikee. Books write vaikea.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Voi ei! means oh no. Here voi is a cry, not the verb voida, can.
Speech drops the d: nähdä becomes nähä. Books write nähdä.
The accusative singular of sinä: sinut, 'you' as the one being seen. Speech says sut.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -ltä for a clock time: kymmenen becomes kymmeneltä, 'at ten'.
Means 'good!' or 'great!', showing you are happy.
Thank you, said by the customer; in casual speech it becomes kiitti.
